the effects of DAO199W on motor function and motor neurons in vivo were most pronounced in females, and that these effects could contribute to an earlier onset of neurological disease in double transgenic female animals compared to SODG93A litter mates.

we have shown that a coding mutation in the gene D-amino acid-oxidase, which causes a change in a single amino acid in the enzyme (DAO R199W) is associated with familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
we have demonstrated in vivo effects of a coding mutation in DAO, associated with ALS, which are most marked in female mice.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying and characterizing the pathogenic effects associated with the in vivo expression DAOR199W and how these effects are influenced by the presence of the SOD1 mutation.
the identification of pathogenetic mechanisms in ALS and the development of new therapeutic approaches to the disease.
the identification and characterization of novel genetic factors that are associated with ALS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DAOR199W has significant effects on motor neuron function and survival in vivo.
the expression of DAOR 199W in vivo in a mouse model, leads to the development of a kyphotic posture and a reduction in the number of spinal cord motorneurons.
DAOR199W expression in vivo, is associated with motor neuron loss and motor dysfunction, which could contribute to an earlier disease onset in female DAOR199W/S0D1G93A double transgenic mice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown the in vivo pathogenic effects of DAOR 199W in the mouse model.
the in vivo effects of the DAOR199 mutation in motor neurons is similar to the effects of DAO overexpression, i.e. loss of motor neurons and motor neuron dysfunction.
DAOR199W expression causes motor neuron loss and motor dysfunction in mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DAOR199 mutation is pathogenic and can cause motor neuron loss in vivo.
we have identified the first genetic cause of ALS linked to the metabolism of a co-agonist of the NMDA receptor.
we identified a potential new target for ALS therapeutics.
